h: Hari Keselamatan Pesakit Sedunia 2026 di The Mall
x: September 2026 · The Mall, Gadong Kami menyertai program kesihatan Hari Keselamatan Pesakit Sedunia (World Patient Safety Day) di The Mall, dengan saringan mata pakai kamera retina, yang mengambil gambar belakang mata. Maklumat di laman ani untuk pendidikan am saja, dan inda menggantikan nasihat doktor abiskita sendiri.

Di klinik mata, abiskita mungkin berjumpa beberapa urang yang lain-lain dalam satu lawatan. Masing-masing ada kerja yang berbeza. Bila abiskita tau siapa siapa, senang abiskita bertanya soalan yang betul. Siapa buat apa? Pakar oftalmologi: doktor mata. Mendiagnosis dan merawat penyakit mata, memberi ubat, dan buat operasi mata Optometris: memeriksa mun abiskita perlu cermin mata atau kanta lekap (dengan temujanji) Ortoptis: memeriksa pergerakan mata, juling, mata malas dan begimbar (nampak dua) (dengan rujukan) Jururawat oftalmik: ubat titis, periksa tekanan mata, dan penjagaan sebelum dan lepas operasi Pembantu oftalmik: ujian penglihatan, imbasan dan ukuran sebelum abiskita jumpa doktor

Pakar oftalmologi (ophthalmologist) atu doktor perubatan yang sudah belajar bertahun-tahun lagi pasal penyakit mata dan operasi mata. Mendiagnosis dan merawat samua penyakit mata, dari mata merah sampai utik (katarak), glaukoma dan penyakit mata kencing manis Memberi ubat titis dan ubat lain Buat operasi mata, rawatan laser dan suntikan mata Mencari tanda penyakit lain yang nampak di mata, macam kencing manis dan darah tinggi Siapa abiskita mungkin jumpa: Pakar Perunding Oftalmologi (consultant, pakar kanan) mengetuai pasukan. Abiskita juga mungkin diperiksa oleh pegawai perubatan (medical officer) dan residen, iaitu doktor yang bekerja dan berlatih di jabatan mata di bawah seliaan pakar perunding.

Optometris (optometrist) dilatih untuk memeriksa mata untuk cermin mata dan kanta lekap. Ani dipanggil refraksi (refraction). Mengukur mun abiskita rabun jauh, rabun dekat atau ada astigmatism Memberi preskripsi cermin mata dan memasang kanta lekap Mungkin membantu dengan alat bantu penglihatan untuk urang yang penglihatannya lemah Di Brunei, optometris di klinik mata kerajaan kebanyakannya buat refraksi saja. Selalunya dorang inda mendiagnosis atau merawat penyakit mata. Mun dorang jumpa masalah dengan kesihatan mata abiskita, dorang akan merujuk abiskita ke doktor mata. Cemana kan jumpa optometris di Brunei? Optometris ada di Klinik Mata Komuniti. Dengan temujanji saja. Inda boleh datang terus (walk-in). Untuk buat temujanji, hubungi pusat kesihatan abiskita dan minta temujanji dengan optometris. Slot temujanji BruHealth atu untuk jumpa doktor, bukan optometris.

Ortoptis (orthoptist) pakar dalam cemana kedua-dua mata bergerak dan bekerja sama-sama. Memeriksa kanak-kanak untuk juling dan mata malas (amblyopia), dan merancang rawatan tampal mata Menilai begimbar pada urang dewasa, contohnya lepas strok atau lumpuh saraf mata, atau pasal penyakit mata tiroid Mungkin memasang prisma di cermin mata untuk membantu begimbar Buat ukuran sebelum dan lepas operasi juling Cemana kan jumpa ortoptis? Dengan surat rujukan saja, dari doktor mata atau optometris.

Jururawat oftalmik atu jururawat yang ada latihan tambahan dalam penjagaan mata. Menitis ubat titis mata, termasuk ubat untuk membesarkan anak mata sebelum doktor memeriksa Membantu di dewan bedah dan klinik suntikan Menyediakan abiskita untuk operasi mata dan menerangkan cemana kan jaga mata lepas atu Mengajar abiskita cemana kan titis ubat mata dengan betul Selalunya urang pertama yang abiskita boleh tanya mun ada soalan atau risau lepas rawatan

Pembantu oftalmik (ophthalmic assistant, atau juruteknik oftalmik) membantu dengan ujian sebelum abiskita jumpa doktor. Memeriksa penglihatan dengan carta huruf Mengukur tekanan mata Mengambil imbasan dan gambar belakang mata (macam OCT dan gambar retina) Buat ujian medan penglihatan (penglihatan tepi) dan ukuran sebelum operasi utik Ujian-ujian ani memberi doktor maklumat yang diperlukan, jadi lawatan boleh rasa lama. Bawa bahan bacaan dan sediakan masa beberapa jam, lagi-lagi mun anak mata abiskita dibesarkan.

Pakar optik (optician) atu lain dari optometris. Selalunya dorang bekerja di kedai cermin mata. Membuat dan memasang cermin mata ikut preskripsi Membantu abiskita memilih bingkai dan kanta Membetulkan dan membaiki cermin mata Dorang inda memeriksa kesihatan mata abiskita.

Penglihatan kabur yang mungkin boleh dibetulkan dengan cermin mata? Jumpa optometris untuk ujian cermin mata. Buat temujanji melalui pusat kesihatan, pasal inda boleh datang terus. Mata merah dan sakit, penglihatan tiba-tiba berubah, atau sudah ada penyakit mata? Jumpa doktor mata (pakar oftalmologi). Abiskita boleh terus datang ke Klinik Mata Komuniti, inda payah surat rujukan. Anak juling atau mata malas, atau begimbar? Jumpa doktor mata dulu. Doktor akan merujuk abiskita ke ortoptis mun perlu. Kecemasan, macam tiba-tiba hilang penglihatan atau mata cedera? Pergi ke Unit Kecemasan hospital atau telefon 991. Klinik Mata Komuniti Maklumat di laman ani untuk pendidikan am saja, dan inda menggantikan nasihat doktor abiskita sendiri.

Panduan ringkas ubat titis mata yang biasa, supaya abiskita tau untuk apa tiap-tiap satu. Sentiasa pakai ubat betul-betul macam yang doktor suruh. Bagus kan tau Warna penutup membantu: penutup ubat titis mata ikut kod warna antarabangsa, contohnya merah jambu untuk steroid dan hijau kebiruan untuk banyak ubat glaukoma Kotak abiskita mungkin nampak lain ikut jenama, jadi sentiasa tengok nama ubat Jangan berkongsi ubat titis mata, dan buang 4 minggu lepas dibuka kecuali label bilang lain Bawa samua ubat titis abiskita tiap-tiap kali datang klinik

1 Basuh tangan. Goncang botol mun label bilang "shake well". 2 Dongakkan kepala dan tarik perlahan kelopak mata bawah sampai jadi poket kecil. 3 Titiskan satu titis ke dalam poket atu. Jangan biarkan hujung botol kena mata atau bulu mata. 4 Tutup mata 1 hingga 2 minit dan tekan perlahan penjuru dalam mata, dekat hidung. Ani supaya ubat inda keluar. 5 Pakai lebih dari satu jenis ubat titis? Tunggu lebih kurang 5 minit antara tiap-tiap jenis.

Dipakai untuk melegakan mata yang kering, berpasir atau penat. Banyak yang boleh dibeli di farmasi. Inda ada warna penutup yang tetap. Tears Naturale Air mata tiruan Ubat titis pelincir untuk mata kering. Selalunya dipakai sampai 4 hingga 6 kali sehari, atau bila perlu. 💡 Perlu lebih dari 6 kali sehari? Tanya pasal ubat titis tanpa pengawet, yang lebih lembut. Lacri-Lube Salap pelincir Salap pekat untuk mata yang sangat kering, selalunya dipakai waktu malam. 💡 Penglihatan jadi kabur sekejap lepas pakai, jadi pakai sebelum tidur.

Untuk merawat atau mencegah jangkitan mata, contohnya konjunktivitis bakteria, ulser kornea, dan lepas operasi mata. Warna penutup: coklat cerah. Chloramphenicol Ubat titis dan salap Untuk jangkitan bakteria macam mata merah yang bertahi mata. Salap selalunya dipakai waktu malam. 💡 Habiskan ubat macam yang doktor suruh. Jangan simpan ubat lebihan untuk lain kali. Fusidic acid Jenama biasa: Fucithalmic Ubat titis antibiotik yang pekat untuk konjunktivitis bakteria, selalunya dipakai dua kali sehari. 💡 Keluar macam gel dan cair dalam mata lepas beberapa saat. Oxytetracycline Jenama biasa: Salap Terramycin Salap antibiotik untuk jangkitan kelopak dan mata, macam pitutan yang berjangkit dan blefaritis. 💡 Sapu sikit di dalam kelopak bawah atau di tepi kelopak, macam yang doktor tunjukkan. Tobramycin Jenama biasa: Tobrex Untuk jangkitan bakteria, termasuk lepas operasi mata. 💡 Rasa pedih sekejap atu biasa. Moxifloxacin Jenama biasa: Vigamox Antibiotik yang kuat untuk jangkitan yang lebih teruk macam ulser kornea, dan untuk mencegah jangkitan lepas operasi. 💡 Untuk ulser kornea, mungkin perlu dipakai kerap banar, sampai tiap-tiap jam pada awalnya. Ikut betul-betul arahan doktor.

Untuk mengurangkan radang (bengkak), contohnya lepas operasi utik (katarak), atau uveitis. Warna penutup: merah jambu. Fluorometholone Jenama biasa: FML Steroid yang lebih lembut untuk radang mata dan setengah alahan. 💡 Goncang dulu sebelum pakai. Dexamethasone Jenama biasa: Maxidex Steroid yang kuat, selalu dipakai lepas operasi mata dan untuk uveitis. 💡 Goncang dulu. Jangan berhenti tiba-tiba kecuali doktor suruh. Dexa + antibiotik Jenama biasa: Maxitrol Steroid yang dicampur dengan antibiotik (neomycin dan polymyxin B), untuk radang bila jangkitan juga perlu dicegah. 💡 Goncang dulu. Pakai selama yang disuruh saja. Prednisolone Jenama biasa: Pred Forte Steroid yang kuat, selalu dipakai lepas operasi utik dan untuk uveitis. 💡 Goncang dulu, pasal ia cecair yang keruh. Dos selalunya dikurangkan sikit-sikit.! Ubat titis steroid perlu preskripsi doktor. Mun dipakai lama, atau tanpa doktor mata memeriksa, ia boleh menaikkan tekanan mata (glaukoma), menyebabkan utik, dan membuat setengah jangkitan, macam herpes atau ulser kulat, jadi lagi teruk banar. Jangan pakai ubat steroid lebihan atau pinjam urang.

Dipakai untuk membesarkan anak mata masa pemeriksaan mata, dan untuk merehatkan mata yang sakit dalam uveitis atau lepas cedera. Warna penutup: merah. Cyclopentolate Jenama biasa: Cyclogyl Membesarkan anak mata dan merehatkan fokus, selalunya untuk pemeriksaan mata kanak-kanak (untuk cermin mata). Hilang dalam kira-kira sehari. 💡 Penglihatan kabur dan silau beberapa jam. Pakai cermin mata hitam dan jangan memandu sampai kesannya hilang. Atropine Ubat pembesar anak mata jangka panjang Dipakai dalam uveitis untuk melegakan sakit, dan kadang-kadang untuk merawat mata malas. Dos yang sangat rendah dipakai untuk memperlahankan rabun jauh kanak-kanak. 💡 Ubat kekuatan penuh boleh bertahan 1 hingga 2 minggu. Basuh tangan lepas pakai dan jauhkan dari kanak-kanak, sebab ia berbahaya kalau tertelan.

Untuk menurunkan tekanan dalam mata dan melindungi saraf mata. Selalunya dipakai tiap-tiap hari, seumur hidup, walaupun abiskita rasa sihat. Latanoprost Jenama biasa: Xalatan Menurunkan tekanan mata. Dipakai sekali sehari, waktu malam. 💡 Simpan botol yang belum dibuka dalam peti sejuk. Lama-kelamaan ia boleh memanjangkan bulu mata dan menggelapkan bahagian mata yang berwarna. Timolol Jenama biasa: Timoptol Menurunkan tekanan mata. Selalunya sekali atau dua kali sehari. 💡 Kasi tau doktor mun abiskita ada lelah (asthma), COPD, atau degupan jantung yang perlahan, pasal timolol mungkin inda sesuai. Brimonidine Jenama biasa: Alphagan Menurunkan tekanan mata. Selalunya dua kali sehari. 💡 Boleh membuat rasa penat, mulut kering atau mata merah dan gatal (alahan). Inda sesuai untuk bayi dan budak kecil. Travoprost + timolol Jenama biasa: DuoTrav Dua ubat glaukoma dalam satu botol, dipakai sekali sehari. 💡 Sama macam timolol: kasi tau doktor kalau abiskita ada lelah (asma), COPD atau degupan jantung perlahan. Brinzolamide Jenama biasa: Azopt Menurunkan tekanan mata. Selalunya dua kali sehari. 💡 Goncang dulu. Penglihatan mungkin kabur sekejap, dan setengah urang rasa pahit di mulut. Terlupa satu dos? Pakai bila abiskita ingat, kecuali sudah hampir masa dos seterusnya. Jangan pakai dua kali ganda. Jangan berhenti ubat glaukoma tanpa bincang dengan doktor mata.

Mun ubat titis membuat mata merah banar, gatal, bengkak atau sakit, berhenti dan hubungi klinik abiskita. Inda pasti pasal ubat abiskita? Tanya ahli farmasi, jururawat mata atau doktor, atau bawa ke Klinik Mata Komuniti. Klinik Mata Komuniti
Terokai model mata 3D. Pusingkan, zum, tengok ke dalam, dan lihat macam mana penyakit mata yang biasa mengubah mata.

Ani model ringkas untuk belajar. Mata dan penyakit sebenar nampak berbeza bagi setiap orang. Kalau penglihatan abiskita berubah, periksa mata. Perubahan tiba-tiba ialah kecemasan: pergi ke Jabatan Kecemasan atau telefon 991.

Ani apa yang abiskita boleh jangka untuk empat prosedur mata yang biasa dibuat di Brunei. Sekilas pandang Suntikan mata memasukkan ubat ke dalam mata untuk mengurangkan bengkak dan salur darah yang bocor di belakang mata Operasi utik menukar kanta yang keruh dengan kanta tiruan yang jernih, selalunya balik hari atu jua Bekikis membuang kurita, lepas atu tempat atu ditutup dengan tisu sihat abiskita sendiri Laser PRP menutup salur darah yang inda normal pasal kencing manis, supaya penglihatan terjaga

Apa kan ani? Ubat dicucuk ke dalam jeli di dalam mata untuk mengeringkan bengkak dan menghentikan salur darah yang bocor [1]. Ubat yang biasa dipakai ialah bevacizumab ("Avastin"). Ada jua ubat lain macam aflibercept, ranibizumab dan faricimab. Kenapa dibuat? Degenerasi makula basah (wet AMD) Bengkak makula pasal kencing manis (diabetic macular oedema) Salur darah retina tesumbat (retinal vein occlusion) Pada hari atu Mata dititis ubat kebas dulu, lepas atu dibersihkan dengan ubat antiseptik (iodin). Suntikan pakai jarum yang halus banar dan ambil beberapa minit saja. Kebanyakan urang rasa tekan saja, inda sakit. Selalunya abiskita perlu beberapa kali suntikan, selalunya tiap-tiap bulan dulu, lepas atu dijarakkan mun mata sudah stabil. Lepas atu Mata rasa berpasir sehari dua atu biasa (selalunya pasal iodin). Tompok merah di bahagian putih mata atu biasa dan inda bahaya. Ia hilang dalam 1 hingga 2 minggu. Nampak bintik terapung (floaters) beberapa hari boleh jadi biasa. Risiko yang mungkin Jangkitan di dalam mata (endoftalmitis): jarang, tapi serius. Tekanan mata naik sekejap, atau jarang-jarang retina tertanggal.! Mun mata abiskita makin sakit, makin merah atau penglihatan makin kabur dalam beberapa hari lepas suntikan, ani mungkin jangkitan. Pergi periksa hari atu jua di klinik mata atau Unit Kecemasan hospital, atau telefon 991. Degenerasi Makula

Apa kan ani? Kanta yang keruh dipecahkan dengan gelombang bunyi dan disedut keluar ( fakoemulsifikasi, atau "phaco"), lepas atu kanta tiruan yang jernih dimasukkan [2][3]. Kenapa dibuat? Bila utik membuat penglihatan keruh atau malap dan mengganggu kehidupan harian. Abiskita inda payah tunggu utik "masak". Pada hari atu Dibuat sebagai kes harian (balik hari atu jua) dengan bius setempat (abiskita sedar, tapi mata kebas). Operasi atu selalunya ambil lebih kurang 20 hingga 30 minit saja. Lepas atu Pakai ubat titis antibiotik dan steroid lebih kurang 4 minggu. Jangan berhenti awal. Pakai pelindung mata waktu tidur, jangan gosok mata, dan jangan biarkan air dan sabun masuk mata. Selalunya abiskita diperiksa tiga kali: Hari 1 Esok hari lepas operasi. Doktor memeriksa penglihatan, tekanan mata dan luka. Hari 7 Lebih kurang seminggu lepas atu. Doktor memeriksa mata sudah sembuh, dan ubat titis mungkin ditukar. Hari 30 Lebih kurang sebulan lepas atu. Doktor memeriksa penglihatan akhir, ubat titis selalunya dihentikan, dan abiskita dikasi tau bila boleh buat cermin mata baru. Risiko yang mungkin Jangkitan, radang atau tekanan mata naik. Retina tertanggal (jarang): tiba-tiba nampak kilat cahaya, banyak bintik terapung baru atau macam tirai gelap mesti diperiksa hari atu jua. Lepas beberapa bulan atau tahun, uncang kanta boleh jadi keruh ( posterior capsule opacification). Ani dibaiki dengan laser YAG yang cepat dan inda sakit. Utik (Katarak)

Apa kan ani? Kurita dibuang, lepas atu sekeping nipis tisu yang sihat dari bawah kelopak mata atas abiskita dipakai untuk menutup tempat atu ( cantuman konjunktiva) [4]. Kenapa dibuat? Bila kurita tumbuh ke tengah mata, mengganggu penglihatan, atau membuat mata inda selesa banar. Pada hari atu Dibuat sebagai kes harian dengan bius setempat. Abiskita balik dengan mata ditutup. Lepas atu Pakai ubat titis steroid untuk beberapa minggu, dikurangkan sikit-sikit, pasal ia membantu supaya kurita inda tumbuh balik. Mata rasa berpasir dan nampak merah selama 1 hingga 2 minggu. Ani biasa. Jangan gosok mata, pasal menggosok boleh mengalihkan cantuman. Risiko yang mungkin Kurita boleh tumbuh balik. Pakai cermin mata hitam dan topi bila di luar, seumur hidup. Ubat titis steroid boleh menaikkan tekanan mata, jadi jangan tinggal temujanji periksa. Kurita (Pterigium)

Apa kan ani? Banyak titik laser yang halus dibuat di bahagian tepi retina. Ani membuat salur darah baru yang inda normal mengecut dan berhenti tumbuh [5][6]. Kenapa dibuat? Retinopati kencing manis proliferatif, bila salur darah baru yang rapuh tumbuh dan boleh berdarah. Setengah kes salur darah retina tesumbat. Pada hari atu Dibuat di klinik. Lepas mata dititis ubat kebas, kanta khas diletak di atas mata abiskita. Ia boleh rasa inda selesa atau ngilu. Abiskita mungkin perlu beberapa sesi. Lepas atu Penglihatan kabur dan silau untuk beberapa jam. Jangan memandu hari atu: bawa urang menemani abiskita. Mun mata rasa ngilu sikit, boleh makan ubat sakit biasa macam paracetamol. Risiko yang mungkin Penglihatan di tepi dan penglihatan waktu malam mungkin berkurang sikit. PRP melindungi dari hilang penglihatan yang teruk. Selalunya ia inda membuat penglihatan lagi terang. Eye conditions grouped by the part of the eye they affect. Tap a number on the eye, or scroll down to choose a topic. We will add more topics to each group over time.! Sudden loss of vision, a very painful red eye, or an eye injury? This is an emergency. Go to the hospital Emergency Department now or call 991. Acute Eye Conditions

The lens sits behind the coloured part of your eye and focuses light. When it turns cloudy, this is called a cataract. Lens Cataract Cloudy, blurred or faded vision that slowly gets worse. Very common with age, and surgery works well.

The optic nerve carries pictures from your eye to your brain. Glaucoma damages this nerve, often because the pressure inside the eye is too high. Optic nerve Glaucoma The "silent thief of sight" that takes side vision first. Find out who should be checked.

The cornea is the clear window at the front of your eye, and the conjunctiva is the thin clear skin over the white of the eye. Both must stay healthy for you to see well. Cornea Dry Eye Gritty, burning or watery eyes? Learn the causes of dry eye and simple treatments that really help. Cornea Digital Eye Strain Tired, dry, sore eyes after long hours on screens. Simple habits like the 20-20-20 rule help. Cornea Conjunctivitis (Pink Eye) Red, watery or sticky eyes from viruses, bacteria or allergy. Most settle on their own; know the red flags. Cornea Pterygium A fleshy growth from the white of the eye onto the cornea, linked to sun, wind and dust. Cornea Contact Lens Safety Wear and care for lenses safely: no tap water, no sleeping in them, and act fast on a red eye. Cornea Corneal Ulcer An infected sore on the clear window of the eye. Contact lens wearers are most at risk. Needs same-day treatment. Cornea Keratoconus The cornea thins into a cone, blurring vision in young people. Cross-linking can stop it worsening.

The retina is the thin, light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, like the film in a camera. Retina Diabetic Retinopathy Diabetes can damage the back of your eye with no early warning. Yearly screening protects your sight. Retina Age-related Macular Degeneration AMD blurs your central vision after 50. Sudden wavy lines need checking within days. Retina Hypertensive Retinopathy High blood pressure can quietly damage the blood vessels in your eyes. Controlling it protects your sight.

Problems with the nerves and brain pathways that control vision, eye movements, the pupils and the eyelids. Nerves Ptosis (Droopy Eyelid) A drooping upper eyelid. Usually due to age, but sometimes a sign of a nerve problem that needs urgent care. Nerves Bell's Palsy and Your Eye Sudden one-sided face weakness can stop the eye closing. Rule out stroke, start treatment early, protect the eye. Nerves Eye Nerve Palsies (3rd, 4th, 6th) Sudden double vision can mean an eye nerve has stopped working. Know when it is an emergency.

The eyelids, tear ducts and eye socket (orbit) protect the eye and keep it moist. Eyelids Blepharitis Sore, gritty, crusty eyelids? Daily warm compresses and lid cleaning keep this long-term condition under control. Eyelids Stye and Chalazion Painful red or firm painless eyelid lumps. Most settle with warm compresses, so never squeeze them. Eyelids Ectropion and Entropion When the eyelid turns outward (ectropion) or inward (entropion), causing watering, redness and irritation. Orbit Thyroid Eye Disease Bulging, red, gritty eyes or double vision with thyroid problems. Stopping smoking helps; faded vision is urgent.

The uvea is the middle layer of the eye, including the coloured iris. Uveitis is inflammation (swelling) of this layer. Uvea Anterior Uveitis A painful red eye with light sensitivity and blurred vision. Needs prompt treatment to protect your sight.

Children's eyes are still developing. Problems caught early, before about age 7, are much easier to treat. Children Myopia in Children Far things look blurry. Often starts at school age. Time outdoors and myopia control can slow it down. Children Amblyopia (Lazy Eye) Weak vision in one eye that often shows no signs. Early glasses, patching or drops work best before 7–8. Children Squint in Children When the eyes do not point the same way. Early treatment helps prevent a "lazy eye". Children Retinoblastoma A rare eye cancer in young children. A white pupil in flash photos needs an eye check within days. This page is for general education and does not replace advice from your own doctor.

Some eye problems are emergencies. Treatment within hours can save your sight. Learn the warning signs, so you know when not to wait.! Do not wait for a clinic appointment. If you have sudden loss of vision, a curtain or shadow over your vision, a very painful red eye, or worsening pain after eye surgery or an eye injection, go to the hospital Emergency Department now or call 991.

h: Warning signs to act on today
x: Sudden blurred vision or loss of vision, in one or both eyes A shower of new floaters, flashes of light, or a dark curtain or shadow A very painful red eye, especially with headache, vomiting or rainbow haloes around lights Pain, redness and worse vision in the days after eye surgery or an eye injection Any injury to the eye, or chemicals in the eye (rinse with plenty of clean water first) Sudden double vision or a suddenly drooping eyelid

Retina Retinal Detachment Flashes, new floaters or a curtain over your vision. The retina is peeling away and needs urgent surgery. Eye pressure Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma Sudden severe eye pain, a red eye, blurred vision, headache and vomiting. Eye pressure rises very fast. Infection Endophthalmitis A serious infection inside the eye, most often days after eye surgery or an eye injection. Eye injury Eye Injuries Blunt, sharp or chemical injuries to the eye. For chemicals, rinse with clean water for 15 minutes, then go to Emergency.

You can walk in to any Community Eye Clinic during office hours to see an eye doctor, no referral letter needed. Community Eye Clinics This page is for general education and does not replace advice from your own doctor.
Want your eyes checked? No referral letter needed. Just walk in to any of these Community Eye Clinics and you will be seen by an eye doctor (an ophthalmology specialist and their team).

h: What is a Community Eye Clinic?
x: Community Eye Clinics are walk-in eye clinics held at health centres. The eye doctors come to a health centre near you, so the public can get a specialist eye review without waiting for a referral letter. This service is unique to Brunei Darussalam. In most other countries, patients first see a general doctor, ask for a referral, and wait for a hospital appointment before they can see an eye specialist. In Brunei, you can walk straight in.

Anyone. It does not matter where you live. You can go to any Community Eye Clinic, even if it is not your own health centre. Come if you have an eye problem, such as blurred vision, a red or painful eye, new floaters, or any worry about your eyes. If you have diabetes, glaucoma in the family, or are over 40, ask the doctor how often you should have your eyes checked.

Office hours: 7.45 am to 12.15 pm, and 1.30 pm to 4.30 pm. Rimba Health Centre: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday Berakas Health Centre: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Saturday Sengkurong Health Centre: Tuesday, Wednesday, Saturday Muara Health Centre: Thursday Temburong (PIHM Hospital): first and third Saturday of every month
After office hours, on Fridays and on Sundays: go to a hospital Emergency Department. Any emergency: go to the nearest hospital Emergency Department straight away, or call 991.

Nine things about your eyes that you may not know, with a new set every day. Tap a card to reveal the answer. How many did you already know? 💻 #1 Staring at your phone all day? {{TAP}} Try the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. Screens do not damage your eyes, but long use without breaks can cause eye strain. {{SRC}} [1, 2] 🌳 #2 What helps protect children from short-sightedness? {{TAP}} Playing outdoors. In a large school study, children who spent more time outdoors each day were less likely to become short-sighted. Encourage outdoor play every day. {{SRC}} [3] 👶 #3 Are babies born with full-sized eyes? {{TAP}} No. A newborn's eyes are about two-thirds of their adult size, and they keep growing through childhood and puberty. {{SRC}} [2] 🧬 #4 How many genes decide your eye colour? {{TAP}} As many as 16 genes may play a part, which is why eye colour can be hard to predict from the parents' eyes. {{SRC}} [2] 🩺 #5 Can a whole eye be transplanted? {{TAP}} Not yet. A whole eye cannot be transplanted because the optic nerve cannot be reconnected. But the cornea (the clear front window) can be transplanted, and this restores sight for many people. {{SRC}} [2] 🌈 #6 Do colour-blind people see only black and white? {{TAP}} Usually not. Most people with colour blindness see some colours, but find it hard to tell reds and greens apart. It is much more common in men, but women can have it too. {{SRC}} [2] 🩸 #7 Have diabetes and your eyesight is fine. Do you still need eye checks? {{TAP}} Yes, every year. Diabetic eye disease often has no early symptoms. Yearly screening finds it early, when treatment can prevent most serious vision loss. {{SRC}} [4, 5] 👨‍👩‍👧 #8 Glaucoma in the family? {{TAP}} Your own risk is higher. Tell your brothers, sisters and children to get their eyes checked, especially after age 40. Glaucoma takes side vision first, with no pain. {{SRC}} [6, 7] 🛌 #9 Is it OK to sleep in your contact lenses? {{TAP}} Avoid it, unless your eye doctor says your lenses are made for this. Sleeping in lenses raises the risk of a serious eye infection. Never rinse lenses or cases with tap water. {{SRC}} [8] 👓 #10 Is losing your sight just part of getting old? {{TAP}} No. Many eye problems that come with age, like cataract, can be treated, and others can be slowed if they are found early. Regular eye checks matter. {{SRC}} [2] 🌍 #11 How many people in the world have a vision problem? {{TAP}} At least 2.2 billion people. For at least 1 billion of them, the problem could have been prevented or still needs treatment, often just glasses or cataract surgery. {{SRC}} [9] 🍼 #12 Can a baby's eye colour change? {{TAP}} Yes. In the first year of life, the iris slowly makes more pigment (melanin), so a baby's eyes may darken over the first 12 months. {{SRC}} [2] 🔭 #13 How common will short-sightedness become? {{TAP}} Researchers predict that by 2050, about half of the world's population may be short-sighted.

InfoSihat: health information at your fingertips. Maklumat Kesihatan dihujung Jari. InfoSihat is a free website that explains health conditions in simple, everyday language, in English and Bahasa Melayu Brunei. It is written by doctors in Brunei for the people of Brunei.

Our vision To empower every individual in Brunei Darussalam with accessible, accurate, and culturally relevant health information, for a healthier and more informed nation. Our mission InfoSihat is dedicated to improving health literacy across Brunei by providing culturally appropriate, evidence-based and user-friendly health information. Through digital platforms, community outreach and collaboration with healthcare professionals, we aim to promote informed health choices, disease prevention and community well-being.

Health literacy is the ability to find, understand and use health information. In Brunei, many people prefer to read in Malay, yet most reliable health information online is in English, written for other countries, and full of medical terms. Speaking at the 2nd ASEAN Digital Public Health Conference in 2022, the Minister of Health said: "Health literacy is still quite low in the country, and it is hoped that digitisation of public health information will help to 'nudge' the public to take better care of their health." A local study at RIPAS Hospital found that 69.5% of patients with diabetes had inadequate knowledge of their condition. InfoSihat aims to help close that gap, starting with the eye.

At the eye clinic you may see several different people in one visit. Each has a different job. Knowing who is who helps you ask the right questions. Who does what? Ophthalmologist: the eye doctor. Diagnoses and treats eye diseases, prescribes medicine, and does eye surgery Optometrist: checks whether you need glasses or contact lenses (appointment only) Orthoptist: checks eye movements, squints, lazy eye and double vision (referral only) Ophthalmic nurse: eye drops, pressure checks, and care before and after surgery Ophthalmic assistant: vision tests, scans and measurements before you see the doctor

An ophthalmologist is a medical doctor who has done further years of training in eye diseases and eye surgery. Diagnoses and treats all eye conditions, from red eyes to cataract, glaucoma and diabetic eye disease Prescribes eye drops and medicines Does eye surgery, laser treatment and eye injections Looks for signs of other illnesses that show up in the eye, such as diabetes and high blood pressure Who you might meet: a Consultant Ophthalmologist (senior specialist) leads the team. You may also be seen by medical officers and residents, who are doctors working and training in the eye department under the consultant's supervision.

An optometrist is trained to test your eyes for glasses and contact lenses. This is called a refraction. Measures whether you are short-sighted, long-sighted or have astigmatism Prescribes glasses and fits contact lenses May help with low vision aids for people with poor sight In Brunei, optometrists at government eye clinics mainly do refraction. They do not usually diagnose or treat eye diseases. If they find a problem with the health of your eye, they will refer you to the eye doctor. How to see an optometrist in Brunei Optometrists are based at the Community Eye Clinics. It is by appointment only. There is no walk-in service. To book, contact your health centre and ask for an appointment with the optometrist. BruHealth appointment slots are for seeing the doctor, not the optometrist.

An orthoptist specialises in how the two eyes move and work together. Checks children for squint and lazy eye (amblyopia), and plans patching treatment Assesses double vision in adults, for example after a stroke or nerve palsy, or with thyroid eye disease May fit prisms on glasses to help with double vision Does measurements before and after squint surgery How to see an orthoptist: by referral only, from the eye doctor or an optometrist.

Ophthalmic nurses are nurses with extra training in eye care. Put in eye drops, including drops to widen the pupils before the doctor examines you Help in operating theatres and injection clinics Prepare you for eye surgery and explain how to look after your eye afterwards Teach you how to put in your eye drops properly Are often your first point of contact if you have questions or worries after treatment

Ophthalmic assistants (also called ophthalmic technicians) help with tests before you see the doctor. Check your vision with the letter chart Measure your eye pressure Take scans and photographs of the back of the eye (such as OCT and retinal photos) Do visual field tests (side vision) and measurements before cataract surgery These tests give the doctor the information they need, so the visit can feel long. Bring something to read and allow a few hours, especially if your pupils are widened.

An optician is different from an optometrist. Opticians usually work in spectacle shops. Make and fit glasses from a prescription Help you choose frames and lenses Adjust and repair glasses They do not examine the health of your eyes.

Blurred vision that glasses might fix? An optometrist for a glasses test. Book through your health centre, as there is no walk-in. Red, painful eye, sudden vision change, or a known eye disease? An eye doctor (ophthalmologist). You can walk in to a Community Eye Clinic, no referral needed. Child with a squint or lazy eye, or double vision? See the eye doctor first. They will refer you to the orthoptist if needed. Emergency, such as sudden loss of vision or an eye injury? Go to the hospital Emergency Department or call 991. A quick guide to common eye drops, so you know what each one is for. Always use your drops exactly as your doctor told you. Good to know Cap colours help: eye drop caps follow an international colour code, for example pink for steroids and teal for many glaucoma drops Your box may look different depending on the brand, so always check the medicine name Never share eye drops, and throw them away 4 weeks after opening unless the label says otherwise Bring all your drops to every clinic visit

h: How to put in eye drops
x: 1 Wash your hands. Shake the bottle if the label says "shake well". 2 Tilt your head back and gently pull down your lower eyelid to make a small pocket. 3 Squeeze one drop into the pocket. Do not let the bottle tip touch your eye or lashes. 4 Close your eye for 1 to 2 minutes and gently press the inner corner, near your nose. This keeps the drop in the eye. 5 Using more than one drop? Wait about 5 minutes between different drops.

Used to soothe dry, gritty or tired eyes. Many can be bought at a pharmacy. They have no set cap colour. Tears Naturale Artificial tears Lubricating drops for dry eyes. Usually used up to 4 to 6 times a day, or as needed. 💡 Needing them more than 6 times a day? Ask about preservative-free drops, which are gentler. Lacri-Lube Lubricating ointment A thick ointment for very dry eyes, usually used at night. 💡 Vision is blurry for a while after use, so put it in just before you sleep.

Used to treat or prevent eye infections, for example bacterial conjunctivitis, corneal ulcers, and after eye surgery. Cap colour: tan. Chloramphenicol Drops and ointment For bacterial eye infections such as sticky conjunctivitis. The ointment is often used at night. 💡 Finish the course your doctor gives you. Do not keep leftover drops for next time. Fusidic acid Common brand: Fucithalmic Thick antibiotic drops for bacterial conjunctivitis, usually used twice a day. 💡 It comes out like a gel and melts into the eye after a few seconds. Oxytetracycline Common brand: Terramycin ointment Antibiotic ointment for eyelid and eye infections, such as infected styes and blepharitis. 💡 Put a small amount inside the lower eyelid or along the lid edge, as your doctor shows you. Tobramycin Common brand: Tobrex For bacterial eye infections, including after eye surgery. 💡 Mild stinging for a moment is normal. Moxifloxacin Common brand: Vigamox A strong antibiotic for more serious infections such as corneal ulcers, and to prevent infection after surgery. 💡 For corneal ulcers it may be needed very often, even hourly at first. Follow your doctor's plan exactly.

Used to calm inflammation (swelling), for example after cataract surgery, or in uveitis. Cap colour: pink. Fluorometholone Common brand: FML A milder steroid for eye inflammation and some allergies. 💡 Shake well before use. Dexamethasone Common brand: Maxidex A strong steroid, often used after eye surgery and for uveitis. 💡 Shake well. Do not stop suddenly unless your doctor says so. Dexa + antibiotics Common brand: Maxitrol A steroid mixed with antibiotics (neomycin and polymyxin B), for inflammation when infection also needs preventing. 💡 Shake well. Use only for as long as prescribed. Prednisolone Common brand: Pred Forte A strong steroid, often used after cataract surgery and for uveitis. 💡 Shake well, as it is a cloudy liquid. The dose is usually reduced step by step.! Steroid drops are prescription only. Used for a long time, or without an eye doctor checking, they can raise eye pressure (glaucoma), cause cataract, and make some infections, like herpes or fungal ulcers, much worse. Never use leftover or borrowed steroid drops.

Used to widen the pupil for eye checks, and to rest a painful eye in uveitis or after an injury. Cap colour: red. Cyclopentolate Common brand: Cyclogyl Widens the pupil and relaxes focusing, often for eye tests in children to check for glasses. Wears off within about a day. 💡 Vision is blurry and bright light is uncomfortable for some hours. Wear sunglasses and do not drive until it wears off. Atropine Long-acting dilating drop Used in uveitis to ease pain, and sometimes to treat a lazy eye. A very weak (low-dose) form is used to slow short-sightedness in children. 💡 The full-strength drop can last 1 to 2 weeks. Wash your hands after use and keep it away from children, as it is harmful if swallowed.

Used to lower the pressure inside the eye and protect the optic nerve. Usually used every day, for life, even if you feel fine. Latanoprost Common brand: Xalatan Lowers eye pressure. Used once a day, at night. 💡 Keep unopened bottles in the fridge. Over months it can make eyelashes longer and darken the coloured part of the eye. Timolol Common brand: Timoptol Lowers eye pressure. Usually once or twice a day. 💡 Tell your doctor if you have asthma, COPD, or a slow heart rate, as timolol may not be suitable. Brimonidine Common brand: Alphagan Lowers eye pressure. Usually twice a day. 💡 Can cause tiredness, a dry mouth or an itchy red eye (allergy). Not for babies and young children. Travoprost + timolol Common brand: DuoTrav Two glaucoma medicines in one bottle, used once a day. 💡 The same cautions as timolol apply: tell your doctor if you have asthma, COPD or a slow heart rate. Brinzolamide Common brand: Azopt Lowers eye pressure. Usually twice a day. 💡 Shake well. Vision may blur for a moment, and some people notice a bitter taste. Missed a dose? Use it when you remember, unless it is nearly time for the next one. Do not double up. Never stop glaucoma drops without talking to your eye doctor.

If a drop makes your eye very red, itchy, swollen or painful, stop it and contact your clinic. Not sure about your drops? Ask your pharmacist, eye nurse or doctor, or bring them to a Community Eye Clinic. Community Eye Clinics
Explore a 3D model of the eye. Turn it, zoom in, look inside, and see how common eye diseases change the eye.

This is a simplified model made for learning. Real eyes and diseases look different from person to person. If you notice a change in your vision, get your eyes checked. Sudden changes are an emergency: go to the Emergency Department or call 991.

Here is what to expect from four common eye procedures in Brunei. At a glance Eye injections put medicine inside the eye to treat swelling and leaky vessels at the back of the eye Cataract surgery swaps the cloudy lens for a clear artificial one, usually as a day case Pterygium surgery removes the fleshy growth and covers the area with your own healthy tissue PRP laser seals off abnormal blood vessels in diabetic eye disease to protect your sight

What is it? A medicine is injected into the jelly inside the eye to dry up swelling and stop leaky, abnormal blood vessels [1]. A common medicine is bevacizumab ("Avastin"). Others include aflibercept, ranibizumab and faricimab. Why is it done? Wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD) Diabetic macular oedema (swelling of the centre of the retina from diabetes) Retinal vein occlusion (a blocked vein in the retina) On the day Numbing drops go in first, then an antiseptic (iodine) to clean the eye. The injection uses a tiny needle and takes only a few minutes. Most people feel pressure, not pain. You usually need a course of injections, often monthly at first, then spaced out if the eye is stable. Afterwards A gritty feeling for a day or so is common (often from the iodine). A red spot on the white of the eye is common and harmless. It fades in 1 to 2 weeks. Some floaters for a few days can be normal. Possible risks Infection inside the eye (endophthalmitis): rare but serious. A short rise in eye pressure, or rarely retinal detachment.! If you have increasing pain, increasing redness or vision getting worse in the days after an injection, this may be infection. Get checked the same day at the eye clinic or the hospital Emergency Department, or call 991. Macular Degeneration

What is it? The cloudy lens is broken up with sound waves and removed ( phacoemulsification, or "phaco"), and a clear artificial lens is put in [2][3]. Why is it done? When a cataract makes your vision cloudy or dim and affects daily life. You do not need to wait for it to be "ripe". On the day Done as a day case under local anaesthetic (you are awake, but the eye is numb). The operation itself usually takes about 20 to 30 minutes. Afterwards Use your antibiotic and steroid drops for about 4 weeks. Do not stop early. Wear the eye shield at night, do not rub the eye, and keep water and soap out of it. You will usually be seen three times: Day 1 The day after surgery. Vision, eye pressure and the wound are checked. Day 7 About one week later. Healing is checked and drops may be changed. Day 30 About one month later. Final vision is checked, drops are usually stopped, and you are told when to get new glasses. Possible risks Infection, inflammation or raised eye pressure. Retinal detachment (rare): sudden flashes, many new floaters or a dark curtain need checking the same day. Months or years later, the lens bag can turn cloudy ( posterior capsule opacification). It is fixed with a quick, painless YAG laser. Cataract

What is it? The pterygium is removed, and a thin piece of healthy tissue from under your upper eyelid is used to cover the area ( conjunctival autograft) [4]. Why is it done? When the pterygium grows towards the centre of the eye, affects your vision, or is very uncomfortable. On the day Done as a day case under local anaesthetic. You go home with an eye pad. Afterwards Use steroid drops for several weeks, reduced step by step, as they help stop regrowth. The eye feels gritty and looks red for 1 to 2 weeks. This is normal. Do not rub the eye, as rubbing can move the graft. Possible risks The pterygium can grow back. Wear sunglasses and a hat outdoors, for life. Steroid drops can raise eye pressure, so keep every check-up. Pterygium

What is it? Many tiny laser spots are placed on the outer parts of the retina. This makes the abnormal new blood vessels shrink and stop growing [5][6]. Why is it done? Proliferative diabetic retinopathy, where fragile new vessels grow and can bleed. Some retinal vein occlusions. On the day Done in the clinic. After numbing drops, a special contact lens is held on your eye. It can feel uncomfortable or achy. You may need several sessions. Afterwards Vision is blurry and dazzled for a few hours. Do not drive that day: bring someone with you. A mild ache can be eased with simple painkillers like paracetamol. Possible risks Some loss of side vision and night vision. PRP protects against severe vision loss. It does not usually make your vision better. Diabetic Retinopathy
Ask your eye doctor or nurse: no question is too small. In an emergency, go to the hospital Emergency Department or call 991.

At a glance A cataract is clouding of the lens inside the eye, most often due to ageing Vision becomes cloudy, blurred or dim, with glare from lights at night Surgery is the only cure: a quick day operation that replaces the cloudy lens with a clear artificial lens You do not need to wait for a cataract to be "ripe": have surgery when it affects your daily life

Inside your eye, behind the coloured part (iris), there is a clear lens. It works like the lens of a camera, focusing light onto the back of the eye so you see a sharp picture. A cataract is when this lens becomes cloudy. Looking through a cataract is like looking through a dirty or frosted window. Cataracts usually develop slowly over years. They often affect both eyes, but one eye may be worse than the other. Cataract is the leading cause of blindness in the world, even though it can be treated with a simple operation [1]. What causes it? As we get older, the proteins in the lens slowly clump together and the lens becomes cloudy and yellow. This is part of normal ageing. Diabetes, smoking, steroids, injury and UV light can make it happen earlier or faster [2].

Most people will get some cataract as they get older. Your risk is higher if you [2]: are over 60 (age is the biggest risk) have diabetes smoke have used steroid medicines for a long time (tablets, eye drops or inhalers) have had an eye injury, eye surgery or radiation treatment to the head or upper body spend a lot of time in strong sunlight without eye protection (UV light) drink a lot of alcohol have a family history of cataracts Babies and children can get cataracts too. Some babies are born with a cataract (congenital cataract). This needs to be found and treated early, because a child's vision is still developing [6]. If your baby's pupil looks white or grey instead of black, or your child does not seem to follow faces or toys, see a doctor soon.

h: How do I know if I have it?
x: Cataracts are not painful and usually do not make the eye red. Common signs are [3]: Cloudy, blurred or misty vision Glare: car headlights or street lights seem too bright, or have halos around them, making night driving difficult Colours look faded or yellowish Needing brighter light to read Frequent changes to your glasses, which do not seem to help for long Sometimes double vision in one eye An eye doctor or optometrist can see a cataract easily during a painless eye check, usually after putting in drops to widen your pupil. What can happen? A cataract does not damage the eye permanently, but as it gets worse it can: make it hard to read, drive, cook or recognise faces make you unsafe to drive, especially at night increase the risk of falls and accidents make you lose confidence and independence in very advanced cases, cause blindness until the cataract is removed

A cataract on its own is not an emergency. But if you have had cataract surgery recently, a serious infection or other problem can rarely happen and needs treatment the same day.! After cataract surgery, go back to the eye clinic or the hospital Emergency Department immediately (or call 991) if you have increasing pain, vision getting worse, a red eye that is getting worse, or sudden flashes, many new floaters or a dark curtain in your vision. Do not wait for your next appointment. If you have sudden loss of vision, or a painful red eye, this is not caused by cataract. Get checked urgently.

In the early stages, new glasses, brighter lighting and anti-glare sunglasses may help. But surgery is the only way to remove a cataract [2]. When should I have surgery? You do not need to wait for the cataract to be "ripe" (very thick). This is an old belief. Surgery is offered when the cataract affects your daily life, such as reading, driving, working or looking after yourself [3][7]. In fact, very advanced cataracts can make surgery harder. The operation The most common method is phacoemulsification (phaco for short). The surgeon makes a tiny cut in the eye, uses sound waves to break up the cloudy lens, and removes it. A clear artificial lens (intraocular lens, or IOL) is put in its place. It stays in the eye for life. It is usually done under local anaesthetic (eye drops or an injection to numb the eye). You are awake but should not feel pain. It usually takes less than an hour, and most people go home the same day (day case) [4]. If both eyes need surgery, they are usually done on different days. Cloudy again after months or years? Some people find their vision slowly becomes cloudy again. This is usually posterior capsule opacification (PCO), sometimes called a "secondary cataract". The thin bag that holds the new lens becomes cloudy. It is not the cataract coming back, and it is fixed with a quick, painless YAG laser treatment in the clinic [4][5].

h: Caring for your eye after cataract surgery
x: Most people recover quickly, and many notice brighter, clearer vision within a few days. Good care in the first month helps your eye heal well and lowers the risk of infection [4][5]. Your check-up appointments In Brunei, you will usually be seen three times after surgery. Your clinic may give you slightly different dates, so always follow the appointment card you are given. Day 1 The day after surgery. The doctor checks your vision, the eye pressure and the wound, and makes sure there is no early infection. You start or continue your eye drops. Day 7 About one week later. The doctor checks that the eye is healing, the inflammation is settling and there is no infection. Your drops may be changed. Day 30 About one month later. The doctor checks your final vision. Your drops are usually stopped, and you are told when to get new glasses, and plans are made for your other eye if needed. Your eye drops You will usually be given antibiotic drops (to prevent infection) and anti-inflammatory drops (steroid drops, to calm the swelling). Most people use them for about 4 weeks, often reducing them step by step. Wash your hands before putting in drops. Do not let the bottle tip touch your eye. If you use more than one type of drop, wait about 5 minutes between them. Do not stop early, even if your eye feels fine. Bring all your drops to every check-up. Protecting your eye Wear the eye shield at night for the first week, or as your doctor advises, so you do not rub your eye in your sleep. Do not rub or press on your eye. Clean around the eye gently with cooled boiled water and clean cotton wool, wiping from the nose outwards. Do not wash inside the eye. For the first 2 to 4 weeks Keep soap, shampoo and water out of the eye. You can shower or bathe, but keep your eye closed and avoid splashing your face. Taking wudhu? Wipe around the eye gently with a damp hand instead of splashing water into the operated eye. Ask your doctor or religious teacher if you are unsure. No swimming, and avoid dusty or smoky places, gardening and dirty water. Avoid heavy lifting and straining for the first week. Do not wear eye make-up. You can read, watch TV, use your phone and walk as normal. Drive only when your doctor says your vision is good enough. What is normal? For the first few days, it is normal for the eye to feel a little gritty, watery or sensitive to light, and for vision to be slightly blurred. Colours may look brighter or bluer than before. This settles as the eye heals. What is not normal? Increasing pain, vision getting worse, a redder eye, or flashes, many new floaters or a dark curtain need checking the same day (see "When to get help urgently" above). New glasses: you may need new glasses, especially for reading. Wait until your doctor says the eye has settled, usually after the Day 30 check, before you get an eye test for glasses.

There is no proven way to stop age-related cataract, but you may be able to slow it down: Stop smoking. Keep diabetes well controlled. Wear sunglasses and a hat in strong sun. Do not use steroid medicines or eye drops unless a doctor prescribed them. Wear eye protection for sports, DIY and work with tools. Have regular eye checks, especially if you are over 60 or have diabetes. Where to get help in Brunei If your vision is getting cloudy or blurred, you can walk in to a Community Eye Clinic at your health centre. No referral is needed. They can check your eyes and refer you for surgery if needed. Community Eye Clinics For emergencies after eye surgery, especially after clinic hours, go to the hospital Emergency Department or call 991.

Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve, the "cable" that carries pictures from your eye to your brain. Once nerve fibres are damaged, they do not grow back, so the vision lost from glaucoma is permanent. Glaucoma is often linked to high pressure inside the eye. Your eye is always making a clear fluid, and the fluid drains out through a tiny drain at the front of the eye. If the drain does not work well, the pressure can build up and press on the optic nerve. Some people get glaucoma even with normal eye pressure. The main types Open-angle glaucoma: the drain slowly becomes less efficient over many years. It is painless and has no early symptoms. Side vision is lost first. Angle-closure glaucoma: the coloured part of the eye (iris) blocks the drain. This can happen slowly, or suddenly as an emergency ("acute attack"). It is more common in people of East and Southeast Asian descent. Other types: glaucoma with normal eye pressure, glaucoma caused by other problems (eye injury, long-term steroid use, advanced diabetic eye disease), and rare glaucoma in babies and children. What causes it? The optic nerve is damaged, most often because the pressure inside the eye is too high for that nerve to cope with. Why this happens is not fully understood. Age, genes (it runs in families), the shape of your eye, and other health conditions all play a part.

Anyone can get glaucoma, but your risk is higher if: you are over 40 a parent, brother or sister has glaucoma you have high eye pressure you are of Asian or African descent you are very short-sighted (open-angle) or long-sighted (angle-closure) you have diabetes you use steroid medicines for a long time (eye drops, tablets, inhalers or creams) you have had an eye injury or eye surgery before Closer to home: in a large study of Malay adults aged 40 to 80 in Singapore, about 3 in 100 had glaucoma, and more than 9 in 10 of them did not know they had it.

h: How do I know if I have it?
x: Open-angle glaucoma has no symptoms in the early stages. You will not feel pain, and your central vision stays clear until late. The only way to catch it early is an eye check. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an emergency. Go to the Emergency Department immediately or call 991 if you suddenly have: Read more: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma What happens at a glaucoma check? All of these tests are painless: Eye pressure test (tonometry) Optic nerve check, looking at the back of the eye Visual field test, which maps your side vision; you press a button when you see a light OCT scan, a photo-like scan that measures the nerve fibre layer Gonioscopy, where the doctor uses a special lens to look at the eye's drain What can happen? Glaucoma slowly takes away your side (peripheral) vision first. Many people do not notice until a lot of vision is gone. Without treatment it can lead to: Tunnel vision, like looking through a pipe Bumping into things, falls, and accidents on the road Not being safe to drive Permanent blindness

Treatment aims to lower the eye pressure so the optic nerve is protected. It cannot bring back vision that is already lost, but it can stop or slow down further damage. Large studies have shown that lowering eye pressure slows glaucoma from getting worse. Eye drops: the most common treatment. They must be used every day, for life, even when your eyes feel fine. Laser treatment: Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) helps the drain work better in open-angle glaucoma. It can be a first treatment instead of drops for some people. Laser iridotomy makes a tiny opening in the iris to relieve or prevent angle closure. Surgery: creates a new drainage channel (trabeculectomy), or places a small drainage tube or device. For some people with angle closure, removing the natural lens (like cataract surgery) helps open the drain. Fasting in Ramadan? Do not stop your glaucoma drops on your own. Talk to your eye doctor about the best timing for your drops, and refer to guidance from the religious authorities if you are unsure.

There is no sure way to prevent glaucoma, but you can prevent blindness from it by catching it early: Have an eye check if you are over 40, and regularly after that as advised. If someone in your family has glaucoma, tell your siblings and children to get their eyes checked. If you have glaucoma, use your drops every day and never miss follow-up appointments. Do not use steroid eye drops unless a doctor prescribed them and is checking your eyes. Protect your eyes with goggles during sports, DIY and work with tools. Stay active and keep diabetes and blood pressure under control. Local updates and research Glaucoma is often hidden: in the Singapore Malay Eye Study, more than 90% of people with glaucoma had never been diagnosed. [6] Worldwide: the number of people with glaucoma was projected to reach about 112 million by 2040, with the largest numbers in Asia. [5]

At a glance Dry eye is when your eyes do not make enough tears, or the tears dry up too quickly It is very common, especially as we get older and use screens more Eyes feel gritty, burning or, surprisingly, watery, and vision may blur but clears when you blink Lubricating eye drops, warm compresses and screen breaks help most people A painful red eye, light sensitivity or reduced vision needs a doctor the same day

Every time you blink, a thin layer of tears spreads over the front of your eye (the cornea). This tear film keeps the eye moist, smooth and comfortable, and helps you see clearly [1][2]. Dry eye (also called dry eye disease) happens when [2][3]: your eyes do not make enough tears, or your tears are poor quality and evaporate too fast. This is the most common type, and is often caused by blocked oil glands in the eyelids ( meibomian gland dysfunction). Dry eye is very common and usually long-term. It is rarely serious, but it can be uncomfortable and annoying. With the right care, most people feel much better [1].

Anyone can get dry eye. It is more likely if you [1][2][3]: are older, especially over 50 spend long hours on screens, because you blink less sit in air-conditioning, or in front of a fan or air vent wear contact lenses have blepharitis or blocked eyelid oil glands are a woman, especially after the menopause take certain medicines, such as antihistamines (allergy medicine), some antidepressants, and some glaucoma eye drops have an autoimmune condition, such as Sjögren's syndrome or rheumatoid arthritis have thyroid eye disease have had laser eye surgery (such as LASIK) Blepharitis

h: How do I know if I have it?
x: Dry eye usually affects both eyes. You may notice [1][2]: eyes that feel gritty, sandy, or like something is in the eye burning, stinging or tired eyes watery eyes: when the eye is dry and irritated, it can make extra tears to protect itself (reflex tearing) blurred vision that clears when you blink redness discomfort that is worse with screens, reading, wind or air-conditioning, or later in the day trouble wearing contact lenses An eye doctor can check your tears and the surface of your eye with a microscope (slit lamp), often using a yellow dye (fluorescein).

Dry eye on its own does not usually cause severe pain or loss of vision. These symptoms suggest something else, such as an infection or inflammation, and need checking the same day: a painful red eye sensitivity to light reduced vision that does not clear when you blink eye pain in a contact lens wearer! If you have a painful red eye, sensitivity to light or reduced vision, see an eye doctor the same day. If you wear contact lenses and your eye is painful, take your lenses out and bring them with you. After hours, go to the hospital Emergency Department or call 991.

There is often no quick cure, but dry eye can usually be well controlled [1][3][4]. Things you can do yourself: Lubricating eye drops (artificial tears) from the pharmacy. If you use them more than 4 to 6 times a day, choose preservative-free drops, which are gentler on the eye. Eye gel or ointment at night. These are thicker and may blur your vision for a while, so they are best used before sleep. Warm compresses and lid hygiene every day if you have blepharitis or blocked oil glands: a warm compress for a few minutes, then gently clean the lid edges. Take screen breaks. Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 6 metres (20 feet) away for 20 seconds, and blink fully. Avoid air blowing at your eyes from air-conditioning, fans or car vents. Drink enough water and stay hydrated. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if any of your medicines might be making your eyes dry. Do not stop prescribed medicine without advice. Treatments your doctor may offer: Anti-inflammatory eye drops, such as a short course of steroid drops or cyclosporine drops. Steroid drops should only be used when a doctor is checking your eye. Punctal plugs: tiny plugs placed in the tear drainage holes in the eyelids, so your tears stay on the eye for longer. Treatment of any underlying condition, such as blepharitis or thyroid eye disease. Where to get help in Brunei If your symptoms do not improve with the tips above, you can walk in to any Community Eye Clinic at your health centre. No referral is needed. Community Eye Clinics

At a glance Digital eye strain is tired, dry, sore eyes after long hours on phones, tablets or computers It is very common and usually does not cause lasting harm We blink less when we stare at screens, so the eyes dry out The 20-20-20 rule, good lighting and regular breaks help most people

Digital eye strain (also called computer vision syndrome) is a group of eye and vision symptoms that come from using screens for a long time [1][2]. It can happen with phones, tablets, laptops, computers and gaming. Why does it happen? We blink much less when we focus on a screen, so the front of the eye (the cornea) dries out. The eye muscles work hard to focus up close for a long time without a break. Glare, poor lighting, small text, and holding a phone too close all add strain. Glasses that are out of date, or a focusing problem that has not been corrected, make it worse. Screens do not damage the eye permanently. The symptoms usually go away after resting your eyes [1].

h: How do I know if I have it?
x: You may notice, usually after screen use [2]: Tired, sore or burning eyes Dry, gritty or watery eyes Blurred vision, or vision that is slow to clear when you look up from the screen Headaches Neck and shoulder ache from your posture

Small changes make a big difference [1][2][3]: Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something about 6 metres (20 feet) away for 20 seconds. Blink fully and often. Try a few slow, complete blinks every now and then. Hold your screen further away. A computer screen should be about an arm's length away, slightly below eye level. Hold your phone at a comfortable distance, not right up to your face. Make text bigger and reduce glare. Match the screen brightness to the room. Use lubricating eye drops (artificial tears) from the pharmacy if your eyes feel dry. Do not sit directly under an air-conditioning vent or fan. Get your eyes checked. You may need glasses, or new ones, for screen work. Blue light glasses have not been shown to reduce eye strain, so you do not need to buy them for this [1].

See an eye doctor if your symptoms do not get better with the tips above, or if you have: blurred vision that does not clear after resting your eyes double vision a red, painful eye, or sensitivity to light headaches that are getting worse These are not caused by screens and need checking. Go to the hospital Emergency Department or call 991 if you have sudden loss of vision or a very painful red eye.

Children can get digital eye strain too. Long hours of close-up work and too little time outdoors are also linked to short-sightedness (myopia) in children [4]. Encourage breaks and the 20-20-20 rule. Aim for at least 2 hours outdoors every day. Keep phones and tablets at a sensible distance. Myopia in Children Where to get help in Brunei You can walk in to any Community Eye Clinic at your health centre. No referral is needed. Community Eye Clinics

At a glance Conjunctivitis is redness and swelling of the thin clear layer covering the white of the eye It is usually caused by a virus, bacteria or an allergy Most cases are mild and get better on their own in 1 to 2 weeks Infective conjunctivitis spreads easily, so wash your hands and do not share towels Pain, light sensitivity, reduced vision, contact lens wear or a newborn with red eyes need a doctor quickly

The conjunctiva is a thin, clear layer that covers the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids. Conjunctivitis means this layer is inflamed, which makes the eye look pink or red [1][2]. There are three main types [1][2][3]: Viral: the most common type. Often comes with a cold or sore throat. The eye is red and watery. It is very contagious. Bacterial: the eye is red with sticky yellow or green discharge. The eyelids may be stuck together in the morning. It is also contagious. Allergic: caused by things like dust, dust mites, pollen or pet fur. The eyes are very itchy and watery, usually both eyes. It is not contagious.

h: How do I know if I have it?
x: Common signs include [1][3]: A pink or red eye, in one or both eyes Watering, or sticky discharge A gritty or burning feeling Itching, especially with allergy Crusty eyelids, especially when you wake up Mildly swollen eyelids Your vision should stay normal, apart from slight blur from discharge that clears when you blink. Conjunctivitis is usually not painful. Real pain or blurred vision suggests something more serious.

Many other eye problems can look like conjunctivitis but can damage your sight [1][4]. See an eye doctor the same day if you have: Eye pain (not just grittiness) Sensitivity to light Reduced or blurred vision that does not clear with blinking A red eye while wearing contact lenses. Take the lenses out. This could be an infection of the cornea. A very red eye after an injury or chemical splash A newborn baby (under 4 weeks old) with red, sticky or swollen eyes A weak immune system, or symptoms that are getting worse or not better after 1 to 2 weeks Corneal Ulcer! If you have a painful red eye, sensitivity to light, reduced vision, or you wear contact lenses, see an eye doctor the same day. A newborn baby with red or sticky eyes must be checked the same day. After hours, go to the hospital Emergency Department or call 991.

Most conjunctivitis gets better by itself in 1 to 2 weeks [1][4]. To feel more comfortable: Clean the eyelids gently with cotton wool soaked in cooled boiled water. Use a fresh piece for each eye. Use a cool compress on the eyes. Use lubricating eye drops (artificial tears) from the pharmacy. Stop wearing contact lenses until your eyes are completely better. By type: Viral: antibiotics do not help viruses. It can take 2 to 3 weeks to settle. Bacterial: usually settles on its own. Antibiotic drops or ointment may help it clear faster, especially if it is not improving [4]. Allergic: avoid the trigger if you can. Antihistamine eye drops from a pharmacist or doctor ease the itch. Try not to rub your eyes. Do not use steroid eye drops unless an eye doctor has examined you. Do not use leftover or borrowed drops, breast milk or traditional remedies in the eye.

Infective conjunctivitis spreads through hands, towels and tissues [2][3]. To stop it spreading: Wash your hands often with soap and water, especially after touching your eyes. Do not share towels, pillows, face cloths or eye make-up. Do not rub your eyes. Throw away eye make-up and disposable contact lenses used while infected. Stay away from swimming pools until it has cleared. Follow your school or workplace advice about staying home. Where to get help in Brunei For a red eye that is not getting better, you can walk in to any Community Eye Clinic at your health centre. No referral is needed. Community Eye Clinics

At a glance A pterygium is a fleshy growth on the white of the eye that grows onto the clear cornea It is linked to sun (UV) exposure, wind and dust, and is common in sunny tropical countries like ours It is not cancer, and most only need lubricating eye drops Surgery is done if it grows towards the centre or affects your vision Sunglasses and a hat help protect your eyes

A pterygium (say "ter-RIDGE-ee-um") is a pink, fleshy, wing-shaped growth on the white of the eye. It usually starts on the side nearest the nose and slowly grows onto the cornea, the clear window at the front of the eye [1]. It can affect one or both eyes. A pinguecula (say "pin-GWEK-you-la") is a small yellowish bump on the white of the eye that does not grow onto the cornea. It is very common and usually harmless [1]. What causes it? Both are linked to long-term exposure to [1][2]: sunlight (UV light), the biggest cause wind, dust and sand dry eyes They are more common in people who live in hot, sunny countries near the equator, and in people who work outdoors, such as fishermen, farmers and construction workers [2]. A pterygium is sometimes called "surfer's eye".

h: How do I know if I have it?
x: Many people have no symptoms apart from noticing the growth in the mirror. You may have [1]: a red, fleshy patch on the white of the eye eyes that feel gritty, dry, itchy or irritated eyes that get red and sore now and then, especially after sun, wind or dust blurred vision, if the pterygium grows over the centre of the cornea or changes the shape of the cornea (astigmatism) An eye doctor can tell you if you have a pterygium by looking at your eye with a microscope (slit lamp).

Most pterygia grow very slowly, over months to years. But some growths on the eye can look similar and need checking.! See an eye doctor promptly if a growth on your eye is growing quickly, is dark or pigmented, bleeds, or looks unusual, so other growths can be ruled out. If you have sudden eye pain or sudden loss of vision, go to the hospital Emergency Department or call 991.

Many people do not need treatment. Your eye doctor may check it from time to time to see if it is growing [1][3]. Lubricating eye drops (artificial tears) help the gritty, dry feeling. A short course of anti-inflammatory drops may be used if the eye is very red and sore. These should only be used as prescribed by a doctor. Surgery is advised if the pterygium is growing towards the centre of the cornea, affecting your vision, or causing a lot of discomfort. About surgery: The pterygium is removed, and a thin piece of healthy tissue from under your own upper eyelid is moved to cover the area. This is called a conjunctival autograft. This method has a lower chance of the pterygium growing back than removing it alone [3][4]. It is usually done as a day case, with the eye numbed. A pterygium can sometimes come back after surgery, so keep protecting your eyes from the sun afterwards.

h: Caring for your eye after pterygium surgery
x: Most people go home the same day. The eye heals well with good care, and following the advice below also helps stop the pterygium coming back [1][3]. Your check-up appointments Your clinic will give you the exact dates on your appointment card. A typical plan is: Day 1 The day after surgery. The doctor removes the eye pad, checks the wound and the graft, and starts your eye drops. 1 to 2 weeks The doctor checks that the graft is healing and staying in place, and removes stitches if needed. 1 month The doctor checks healing and your eye pressure, and plans how to slowly reduce your drops. 3 to 12 months Regular checks for any sign of the pterygium growing back. Most regrowth happens in the first year. Your eye drops You will usually be given antibiotic drops and steroid drops. Steroid drops calm the swelling and help prevent regrowth, so they are often used for several weeks, reduced step by step. Do not stop early. Steroid drops can raise the eye pressure, so keep every check-up. Wash your hands first, and do not let the bottle tip touch your eye. What is normal? A gritty, scratchy feeling for 1 to 2 weeks, especially if you have stitches. Redness and swelling where the pterygium was. This slowly fades over a few weeks. Watering and mild sensitivity to light. Protecting your eye Do not rub or press the eye. Rubbing can move the graft. Wear the eye shield at night if you are given one. Keep water and soap out of the eye for about 2 weeks. Taking wudhu? Wipe around the eye gently with a damp hand instead of splashing the operated eye. No swimming for about 2 to 4 weeks, and avoid dusty, windy and smoky places. Wear sunglasses and a hat outdoors, now and for life, to lower the chance of regrowth.! See an eye doctor the same day if you have increasing pain, vision getting worse, yellow or green discharge, or the graft looks like it has come loose. After hours, go to the hospital Emergency Department or call 991.

You can lower the chance of a pterygium starting, growing or coming back after surgery [1]: Wear sunglasses that block 100% of UV light, ideally a wraparound style. Wear a wide-brimmed hat or cap outdoors. Protect your eyes from wind and dust, for example with goggles or safety glasses at work or when riding. Use lubricating eye drops if your eyes feel dry. Where to get help in Brunei If you notice a growth on your eye, or your eyes are often red and irritated, you can walk in to any Community Eye Clinic at your health centre. No referral is needed. Community Eye Clinics

At a glance Contact lenses are safe for most people when worn and cleaned correctly Poor lens care can cause a serious eye infection that may lead to blindness Never let lenses touch tap water, and do not sleep or swim in them Coloured or cosmetic lenses bought without an eye check carry the same risks A red, painful eye in a lens wearer needs an eye doctor the same day

Contact lenses are thin lenses worn directly on the cornea, the clear front window of the eye. They correct vision like glasses, and some are used only to change eye colour [1][2]. Main types [2]: Daily disposable soft lenses: worn once and thrown away each night. These need no cleaning and are often the safest choice. Two-weekly or monthly soft lenses: taken out, cleaned and stored every night, then replaced on schedule. Rigid gas permeable (RGP) lenses: small, firm lenses that last longer. They are often used for keratoconus or high prescriptions. Extended wear lenses: approved for overnight wear, but sleeping in any lens raises the risk of infection. Coloured or cosmetic lenses: these are still medical devices and need a proper fitting.

The biggest risk is a corneal infection (microbial keratitis), which can cause a corneal ulcer [1][4]. It can scar the cornea and, in severe cases, cause permanent loss of vision. Your risk is higher if you [1][3][4]: sleep or nap in your lenses swim, shower or use a hot tub with lenses in let lenses or the case touch tap water, or use saliva top up old solution instead of using fresh solution wear lenses longer than advised, or do not replace the lens case buy lenses without a prescription or proper fitting Acanthamoeba is a tiny organism found in tap water, pools, the sea and soil. It can cause a very painful infection that is hard to treat, and it mostly affects contact lens wearers [5]. Corneal Ulcer

h: How do I wear them safely?
x: Follow these simple rules [1][2][3]: Wash and dry your hands before touching your lenses. Never use tap water, bottled water or saliva to rinse or store lenses. Use fresh solution every time. Never top up old solution. Rub and rinse reusable lenses with solution, if your solution instructions say to. Do not sleep in your lenses unless your eye doctor says it is safe. Take them out before swimming or showering. Replace your lenses on time. Clean your case, leave it to air dry, and replace it at least every 3 months. Keep glasses as a backup, and have regular eye checks. If your eye becomes red or uncomfortable, take the lenses out and do not put them back.

Coloured, "costume" or "big eye" lenses look like a fashion item, but they carry the same risks as any contact lens [2][3]. Do not buy them from beauty shops, markets or online sellers without a prescription. Lenses that are not fitted to your eye can scratch the cornea and let germs in. Never share lenses with friends, even once. Have your eyes checked and your lenses fitted by a qualified optometrist or eye doctor.

A lens-related infection can get worse within hours. Do not "wait and see" [1][4]. Warning signs in a lens wearer: Eye pain or a feeling that something is stuck in the eye A red eye Blurred vision Sensitivity to light Watering or discharge A white spot on the clear part of the eye! If you wear contact lenses and have a red, painful eye, sensitivity to light or blurred vision, take your lenses out and see an eye doctor the same day. Bring your lenses and lens case with you. After hours, go to the hospital Emergency Department or call 991. Where to get help in Brunei You can walk in to any Community Eye Clinic at your health centre. No referral is needed. Community Eye Clinics

At a glance A corneal ulcer is an open sore on the clear front window of the eye, usually from an infection It is an eye emergency: you need to be seen by an eye doctor the same day Contact lens wear is the biggest risk, especially sleeping, swimming or showering in lenses Never treat it yourself with old or borrowed eye drops, especially steroid drops

The cornea is the clear, dome-shaped window at the very front of your eye. It lets light in and helps focus it. A corneal ulcer is an open sore on the cornea. Most are caused by an infection, which doctors call infective (microbial) keratitis (keratitis means inflammation of the cornea). Germs that can cause a corneal ulcer include [1][4][5]: Bacteria: the most common cause. Some bacteria can damage the cornea within a day or two. Fungi: often after the eye is scratched by plant material, such as a branch, leaf, thorn or crop. This is more common in farming, gardening and rural areas and in hot, humid tropical countries like ours. Acanthamoeba: a tiny organism found in tap water, pools, the sea, soil and dust. It mostly affects contact lens wearers and can be very hard to treat. Viruses: especially the herpes simplex (cold sore) virus, which can come back again and again. What causes it? The cornea is normally very good at keeping germs out. An ulcer happens when its surface is damaged (by a scratch, a contact lens or dryness), allowing germs to get in and grow. Contact lenses can trap germs against the eye and reduce the oxygen the cornea gets.

Your risk is higher if you [1][2]: wear contact lenses, which is the biggest risk, especially if you: sleep in them (including naps) swim, shower or wash your face with them in rinse lenses or the case with tap water, or top up old solution wear them longer than advised, or do not replace the case have an eye injury, especially from plants, soil or wood have dry eyes, or eyelids that do not close fully use steroid eye drops, especially without a doctor checking your eye have had a cold sore virus infection in the eye before have diabetes or a weak immune system have had eye surgery on the cornea

h: How do I know if I have it?
